items.t: Tesla helped design the AC electricity system used in homes.
items.d: AC means alternating current. The flow of electricity keeps switching direction.

items.t: A Tesla coil makes high-voltage electricity that flips very fast.
items.d: Voltage is the push that moves electric charge. This coil's push is huge.

items.t: The tesla, a unit for how strong a magnet's field is, is named for Nikola Tesla.
items.d: Scientists made it an official unit in 1960.

items.t: Marie Curie was born in Warsaw, Poland, in 1867.
items.d: She became one of the great scientists who studied energy in matter.

items.t: Marie and Pierre Curie shared a Nobel Prize in Physics in 1903.
items.d: They earned it for research on radioactivity, energy some materials give off.

items.t: In 1911 Marie Curie won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
items.d: The prize honored her discovery of the elements radium and polonium.

items.t: Marie Curie was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize.
items.d: A Nobel Prize is one of the highest awards in the world.

items.t: Marie Curie was the first person to win two Nobel Prizes.
items.d: Winning twice means her work was chosen as outstanding in two different years.

items.t: The element polonium was named after Marie Curie's Poland.
items.d: She and Pierre chose the name to honor the country where she was born.

items.t: Radium gets its name from the Latin word for ray.
items.d: In Latin, radius means ray. The name fits an element that sends out rays.

items.t: Marie Curie gave us the word radioactivity.
items.d: It means some materials send out energy on their own.

items.t: At about age five, a compass sparked Einstein's curiosity.
items.d: The needle kept pointing north. He felt a hidden force must move it.

items.t: Einstein examined patents at the Swiss Patent Office in Bern.
items.d: A patent protects a new invention. He studied ideas people sent in.

items.t: 1905 is called Einstein's miracle year.
items.d: He published four huge physics papers in that single year.

items.t: E = mc squared is called the world's most famous equation.
items.d: E is energy, m is mass, and c is the speed of light. Tiny mass, huge energy.

items.t: Einstein won the 1921 Nobel Prize for the photoelectric effect.
items.d: Light can bump electrons, tiny electric bits, out of a piece of metal.

items.t: In 1915 Einstein proposed general relativity, a new idea of gravity.
items.d: It is a deeper picture of the pull that keeps your feet on the ground.

items.t: Einstein's 1917 work on stimulated emission led to lasers.
items.d: A laser makes a thin, bright beam, like the scanner at a shop checkout.

items.t: Hawking predicted that black holes can give off energy.
items.d: Scientists call that energy Hawking radiation.

items.t: From 1979 to 2009 Hawking held the math job Newton once had.
items.d: Both were Lucasian Professor of Mathematics at Cambridge.

items.t: As a teen, Hawking helped build a computer from clock parts.
items.d: They built it from pieces that used to be inside clocks.

items.t: Hawking's book A Brief History of Time was a bestseller.
items.d: It stayed on the Sunday Times list for 237 weeks, about four and a half years.

items.t: One second is defined by 9,192,631,770 microwave oscillations linked to cesium atoms.
items.d: Atomic clocks count these oscillations to keep very accurate time.

items.t: Clocks do not measure time itself. They measure how long it is between two events.
items.d: The time between a race starting and finishing is an interval.

items.t: About 1,900 years ago, Ptolemy split each degree into 60 minutes and each minute into 60 seconds.
items.d: Ptolemy used this idea about 1,900 years ago.

items.t: Old units like the foot and the pace changed from person to person because body sizes differ.
items.d: That made trading tricky, so people wanted fixed standards.

items.t: Since 1983 the metre has been the distance light travels in a vacuum in 1/299,792,458 of a second.
items.d: Light is the ruler now.

items.t: Because light's speed is known exactly, we can measure far distances by timing light or radio signals.
items.d: Signals bounced off the Moon can be timed to find its distance.

items.t: For 130 years, a metal cylinder called Le Grand K was the official kilogram.
items.d: It was the standard from 1889 until 2019.

items.t: Le Grand K was a small cylinder, about 39 millimetres tall and 39 millimetres wide.
items.d: That is a little taller than a big coin is wide.

items.t: One litre of water near 4 C has a mass of almost exactly one kilogram.
items.d: The water in a one-litre bottle has a mass of about one kilogram.

items.t: A litre is the amount of space inside a cube that is 10 centimetres on each side.
items.d: 10 x 10 x 10 = 1,000 cubic centimetres.

items.t: The prefix kilo means 1000, so a kilogram is 1,000 grams.
items.d: A kilometre is 1,000 metres too.

items.t: The prefix milli means one thousandth, so a millimetre is a thousandth of a metre.
items.d: 1,000 millimetres make 1 metre.

items.t: Mass is measured in kilograms, but weight is a force measured in newtons.
items.d: A 1 kg object weighs about 9.8 newtons on Earth.

items.t: The Moon's gravity is about one-sixth of Earth's, so things weigh about a sixth as much there.
items.d: Your mass stays the same, only your weight changes.

items.t: A NASA spacecraft was lost in 1999 because one team used English units and another used metric units.
items.d: Always check which units you are using.

items.t: An inch is exactly 2.54 centimetres.
items.d: So 10 inches is 25.4 centimetres.

items.t: The words inch and ounce both come from Latin uncia, meaning one twelfth.
items.d: The Roman foot was split into 12 parts.

items.t: A fathom is 6 feet, about 1.8 metres, and was mainly used to measure water depth.
items.d: It was first based on the span of a man's outstretched arms.

items.t: If nothing pushes it, an object stays still, or keeps moving straight at a steady speed.
items.d: A soccer ball stops on grass because the grass and the air push against it.

items.t: Inertia means an object resists any change in how it is moving.
items.d: When a bus stops fast, you lean forward. Your body tries to keep moving.

items.t: More mass means more inertia. Heavier things are harder to speed up or slow down.
items.d: An empty backpack is easy to swing. A backpack full of books is not.

items.t: The same push speeds up a light object more than a heavy one.
items.d: Push an empty wagon and a full wagon just as hard. The empty one wins.

items.t: Newton's second law: speed-up depends on mass and on the size of the push.
items.d: Add more push and the speed-up grows. Add more mass and the speed-up shrinks.

items.t: Newton's second law is often written F = ma: force equals mass times acceleration.
items.d: If the total push doubles and the mass stays the same, the speed-up doubles too.

items.t: Momentum is mass times velocity. A heavy and fast object is hard to stop.
items.d: A slow wagon can be hard to stop if it is loaded. Speed and mass both matter.

items.t: A ping-pong ball takes far less effort to stop than a freight train.
items.d: Stopping means changing speed. Less mass means that change takes less effort.

items.t: Newton's third law: every action has an equal and opposite reaction.
items.d: Push on a wall and the wall pushes you back with the same strength.

items.t: Forces never happen alone. They always come in pairs.
items.d: When your foot pushes the ground back, the ground pushes your foot forward.

items.t: The two forces in an action-reaction pair act on two different objects.
items.d: One push acts on you. The other push acts on whatever you pushed.

items.t: A resting book pushes down on the table. The table pushes up equally.
items.d: The downward push acts on the table. The upward push acts on the book.

items.t: A jet engine throws hot gases backward, and the gases push the engine forward.
items.d: That forward push is called thrust, and it is how jet planes gain speed.

items.t: A garden sprinkler spins because spraying water pushes back on the arms.
items.d: Each jet goes one way. The arm is nudged the opposite way, so it turns.

items.t: Leap from a small boat to the dock, and the boat moves the other way.
items.d: Your legs push you toward the dock and push the boat away. Tie it first.

items.t: Water blasting forward out of a hose pushes the hose backward.
items.d: A firefighter has to grip the nozzle hard so the hose does not jump away.

items.t: A squid swims by squeezing a fast jet of water out through a funnel.
items.d: The water shoots one way, so the squid is pushed the opposite way.

items.t: A squid changes direction by pointing its funnel a new way.
items.d: Aim the funnel a different way, and the push on the squid turns too.

items.t: One newton is the force that gives 1 kilogram an acceleration of 1 meter per second each second.
items.d: With no other force, that push makes 1 kg go 1 meter per second faster every second.

items.t: The unit of force called the newton is named after Isaac Newton.
items.d: Scientists name the unit of force after him because of his laws of motion.

items.t: A small apple of about 100 grams weighs about 1 newton on Earth.
items.d: Weight is Earth's pull. Hold a small apple and you are holding about 1 newton.

items.t: With no air resistance, falling objects all speed up at the same rate.
items.d: A big rock and a pebble match. In air, the pebble is slowed more by the air.

items.t: With no air resistance, a thrown object follows a curve called a parabola.
items.d: Toss a ball to a friend. It rises, bends over, and comes down in that curve.

items.t: Gravity pulls the Moon inward and holds it in orbit around Earth.
items.d: Without that pull, the Moon would keep going straight and leave the loop.

items.t: Newton's laws and Kepler's laws explain why planets move in ellipses.
items.d: An ellipse is an oval. Planet paths are ovals, not perfect circles.

items.t: Friction is a force that resists sliding. It also lets us walk.
items.d: Without friction, your foot would slip and you could not push off to walk.

items.t: Starting a slide usually takes more force than keeping the slide going.
items.d: A heavy box is stubborn at first. Once it is moving, a smaller push can keep it going.

items.t: A car's tire grip sets its best speed-up and its shortest stop.
items.d: Icy roads lower that grip. The car gains speed slowly and needs more room to stop.

items.t: A seat belt reel can lock itself when the car slows down very fast.
items.d: Inertia triggers the lock. The belt stops coming out, and you stay with the seat.

items.t: A seat belt spreads out your stop, which makes the force on you smaller.
items.d: A very quick stop needs a huge push. A slightly longer stop is gentler.

items.t: Swedish inventor Nils Bohlin designed the three-point seat belt we use.
items.d: One belt crosses your lap and your chest, held at three places.

items.t: Crumple zones are built to fold in a set way and soak up energy.
items.d: The folding uses up energy, so less of the stop is left as a hard jolt.

items.t: Crumple zones lengthen a stop, so the average force on riders is smaller.
items.d: The car's speed changes by the same amount, but over a longer moment.

items.t: The passenger cabin is a strong safety cell. The front and rear are made to fold.
items.d: Riders stay in the firm middle while the ends fold in a planned way.

items.t: An airbag fills up in about 20 to 30 milliseconds.
items.d: That is about 0.02 to 0.03 seconds. The bag is full almost at once.

items.t: Airbags have vent holes so they deflate as a person presses into them.
items.d: As you press in, air leaves through the holes and your stop is eased.

items.t: An airbag is a helper for a seat belt. It does not replace the belt.
items.d: The belt holds you in place. The bag adds a soft cushion in front.

items.t: A sensor feels a very sudden slowdown, then tells the airbag to fill.
items.d: It is looking for a quick drop in speed before it starts the bag.

items.t: In rowing, the oar works as a lever that pivots in the water to push the boat.
items.d: The oar pivots where it meets the water and levers the boat ahead.

items.t: Between strokes, a racing boat keeps gliding forward. Rowers call this the run.
items.d: After each pull, the boat keeps sliding ahead on its own for a moment.

items.t: Racing rowboats are long and narrow, with a rounded bottom, to cut drag.
items.d: Less drag means the water resists the boat less, so each stroke goes farther.

items.t: A lighter steerer makes a racing boat easier to push forward.
items.d: Less mass needs less force to speed up. Rules set a lowest weight for that person.

items.t: Extra body weight adds drag to a boat, so heavier rowers need more power.
items.d: The added drag slows the boat. Bigger rowers can balance it with stronger strokes.

items.t: Race swimmers try to make as little water resistance as they can.
items.d: Less resistance means the same push gives them more speed.

items.t: Lane lines and a deep pool cut water resistance and make the pool faster.
items.d: Calmer water drags on your body less, so more of your effort becomes speed.

items.t: Starting blocks let swimmers push off with more force and begin faster.
items.d: A firm block gives their feet something solid to drive against.

items.t: On the start block, swimmers press down on bent legs before they launch.
items.d: Pressing first loads the leg muscles so the push-off can be stronger.

items.t: When something is launched forward, a heavier launcher moves back more slowly.
items.d: A heavy cart and a light cart toss the same ball just as fast. The heavy cart rolls back slower.

items.t: A spinning gyroscope resists any change to the direction of its spin.
items.d: It tends to keep its spin axis pointing the same way.

items.t: Aristotle thought things move only while a force keeps pushing them. He was wrong.
items.d: After you let go, a puck on ice keeps sliding. A force is needed to stop it, not to keep it going.

items.t: Momentum is an object's mass times its velocity.
items.d: A heavy truck rolling slowly can have more momentum than a fast tennis ball.

items.t: Momentum has a size and a direction, so it is a vector.
items.d: Two skaters pushing apart have opposite momentum, one goes left and one goes right.

items.t: Momentum is measured in kilogram metres per second.
items.d: A 2 kg ball moving at 3 metres per second has momentum 6 kg m/s.

items.t: A body's momentum changes at a rate equal to the net force pushing on it.
items.d: A harder push changes how much a shopping cart's momentum grows each second.

items.t: In a closed system with no outside forces, the total momentum stays the same.
items.d: Two ice skaters push off each other, and their total momentum is still zero.

items.t: In a closed system, momentum is conserved separately in all three directions.
items.d: Up and down, left and right, and forward and back each keep their own balance.

items.t: Hit a row of swinging balls with one ball, and the middle balls barely move while the last one swings out.
items.d: The momentum travels through the row like a quick message.

items.t: Lift two balls in a Newton's cradle, and two balls swing out on the other side.
items.d: Lift three, and three swing out. The same number come out as go in.

items.t: A Newton's cradle slowly stops as motion energy changes into sound, heat, and other motion.
items.d: It is not a perpetual-motion machine.

items.t: Each hit in a Newton's cradle sends a sound wave through the middle balls.
items.d: That is also why you hear the satisfying click.

items.t: A car crumple zone was invented by an engineer named Bela Barenyi.
items.d: He worked for a car company and patented the idea in the 1950s.

items.t: Bela Barenyi split a car into a rigid passenger cabin and crumple zones at the front and back.
items.d: The cabin stays strong while the ends are made to squash.

items.t: Crumple zones make a crash last longer, which spreads the force over more time.
items.d: Think of catching an egg by pulling your hands back as it lands.

items.t: Crumple zones are weakened on purpose, while the cabin is made strong like a safety cell.
items.d: A crushed front end is the car doing its job.

items.t: An airbag fills with gas in about 20 to 30 thousandths of a second.
items.d: That is much quicker than a blink of an eye.

items.t: Airbags are filled mainly with nitrogen gas, made by a very fast chemical reaction.
items.d: Nitrogen is also the main gas in the air we breathe.

items.t: Airbags are called 'passive' safety devices because people need to do nothing to use them.
items.d: Seat belts are 'active' because you must buckle them.

items.t: When two objects of equal mass collide elastically head on, they swap momenta.
items.d: A moving pool ball can hit a still one and stop, passing its motion on.

items.t: In a closed system, an inelastic collision conserves momentum but not motion energy.
items.d: Some motion energy changes into heat, sound, or changes of shape.

items.t: In a perfectly inelastic collision, the objects stick together after they hit.
items.d: A lump of clay thrown at another lump will stick and move off together.

items.t: Motion energy lost in a collision turns into jiggling atoms, which we feel as heat.
items.d: Smack a lump of clay hard and it warms up a tiny bit.

items.t: Most real-world collisions are partly inelastic.
items.d: Some motion energy changes into other forms, but the objects may still bounce.

items.t: The coefficient of restitution is usually a number between 0 and 1.
items.d: A bigger number means a bouncier collision.

items.t: A coefficient of restitution of 0 means the objects do not bounce at all and stay touching.
items.d: A ball of wet clay dropped on the floor is a good example.

items.t: A ball's drop height and bounce height can be used to find its coefficient of restitution.
items.d: A higher bounce usually means a larger coefficient.

items.t: Impulse is the change in an object's momentum.
items.d: It is measured in newton-seconds, the same unit as momentum.

items.t: Impulse from a steady force equals the force multiplied by how long it acts.
items.d: A force of 10 N for 3 seconds gives an impulse of 30 newton-seconds.

items.t: A golf club hitting a ball is a big force acting for a very short time.
items.d: That quick, strong push gives the ball a lot of momentum.

items.t: A ball that bounces straight back at the same speed changes momentum twice as much as one that stops.
items.d: Reversing direction adds another momentum change.

items.t: Bike helmets have a stiff foam liner that crushes against the head in a hit.
items.d: The foam takes longer to stop your head, which softens the force.

items.t: The modern three-point seat belt was developed by Nils Bohlin and introduced in 1959.
items.d: He worked for a car company in Sweden.

items.t: A three-point seat belt spreads crash forces across the chest, pelvis, and shoulders.
items.d: Spreading the force over a bigger area lowers pressure on each part.

items.t: When a car stops suddenly, passengers keep moving unless a belt supplies a force to stop them.
items.d: The moving passengers have momentum, which is why seat belts matter.

items.t: On 26 September 2022, NASA's DART spacecraft crashed into the asteroid moonlet Dimorphos on purpose.
items.d: It was a test to see if a hit could change an asteroid's motion.

items.t: Benjamin Robins invented the ballistic pendulum in 1742.
items.d: It uses conservation of momentum to measure the momentum of fast objects.

items.t: An orbit is a path that one object repeats around another object in space.
items.d: The Moon follows an orbit around Earth.

items.t: Perigee is a satellite's closest point to Earth. Apogee is its farthest point.
items.d: These words can also describe the Moon's changing distance from Earth.

items.t: A satellite needs the right sideways speed to orbit.
items.d: Too little speed makes it fall down. Too much speed sends it past the planet.

items.t: One trip around Earth in low Earth orbit takes about 90 minutes.
items.d: The International Space Station flies in this region.

items.t: A geostationary satellite orbits every 24 hours above the equator.
items.d: It stays over the same place on Earth.

items.t: Earth is farthest from the Sun during Northern Hemisphere summer.
items.d: This shows that seasons are not caused by Earth's distance from the Sun.

items.t: In a vacuum, gravity makes objects fall at the same rate.
items.d: Air slows a feather more than a hammer, but a vacuum has no air to do that.

items.t: A spacecraft, its crew, and everything inside can fall around Earth together.
items.d: Because they fall together, the crew seems to float inside.

items.t: At the space station's height, Earth's gravity is still about 90 percent as strong as it is on the ground.
items.d: Floating happens because of free fall, not because gravity is weak there.

items.t: A candle flame becomes rounder in microgravity.
items.d: Gravity normally helps give a candle flame its familiar shape.

items.t: Special planes can give passengers about 20 to 30 seconds of free fall at a time.
items.d: The plane creates free fall by flying along an up-and-down arc.

items.t: Drop towers let objects experience free fall.
items.d: Special equipment releases objects from the tops of tall towers.

items.t: Spring tides happen when the Sun and Moon pull together at new moon and full moon.
items.d: High tides become higher, and low tides become lower.

items.t: Spring tides are named for water springing forth, not for the season.
items.d: They happen about twice each month throughout the year.

items.t: Neap tides happen when the Sun and Moon are at right angles.
items.d: They bring milder tides about a week after a spring tide.

items.t: The Moon's gravity creates ocean bulges on two sides of Earth.
items.d: That is why most coasts have two high tides and two low tides each day.

items.t: The Moon's gravity stretches Earth very slightly into a football-like shape.
items.d: Earth becomes a little longer at the equator and shorter at the poles.

items.t: Some large Moon basins hide areas of extra gravity called mascons.
items.d: Mascons can noticeably change a spacecraft's orbit around the Moon.

items.t: Jupiter's gravity near its cloud tops is about 2.4 times Earth's surface gravity.
items.d: It has the strongest gravity of all the planets.

items.t: Saturn's gravity near its cloud tops is about 92 percent of Earth's surface gravity.
items.d: Saturn is huge but has a low density for its size.

items.t: Tiny Mercury and Mars have almost equal surface gravity.
items.d: Each has about 38 percent of Earth's surface gravity.

items.t: Jupiter's escape speed is over five times Earth's, while the Moon's is about one-fifth.
items.d: Escape speed is the speed needed to break free from a world's gravity.

items.t: Mars's two small moons look like potatoes instead of balls.
items.d: They have too little mass for gravity to pull them into spheres.

items.t: Gravity keeps Jupiter's moon Io stirred inside, helping power many volcanoes.
items.d: Io is tugged by giant Jupiter and by the moons Europa and Ganymede.

items.t: The Sun's gravity holds the solar system together.
items.d: The Sun contains about 99.8 percent of the solar system's mass.

items.t: A curveball dips because the pitcher spins the ball forward as it flies.
items.d: Forward spin is called topspin. It pulls the ball downward on the way to the batter.

items.t: Soccer players can bend a free kick by spinning the ball.
items.d: Spin gives the ball a sideways push from the air, so it can curve past a wall of players.

items.t: Topspin makes a tennis ball drop faster than gravity alone would pull it.
items.d: Players use topspin so a hard shot still falls inside the lines of the court.

items.t: Backspin on a golf ball makes a small upward push against gravity.
items.d: That little lift helps the ball stay in the air a bit longer than it would with no spin.

items.t: A spinning ball drags nearby air with it, and pressure pushes the ball sideways.
items.d: The spin speeds air on one side and slows it on the other. The two pressures are not equal.

items.t: On a spinning ball, the air's push is at a right angle to the flight.
items.d: The push is also at a right angle to the spin's axis, so the ball can lift, dip, or curve.

items.t: Raised stitches on a baseball stir up the air that flows past the ball.
items.d: The stitches stick out and disturb the thin layer of air hugging the leather.

items.t: If we ignore air, a thrown or kicked ball follows a curve called a parabola.
items.d: The ball rises, slows at the top, then comes down, like water from a hose.

items.t: With no air resistance, a ball keeps the same sideways speed for the whole flight.
items.d: No push speeds it up or slows it sideways, so that part of the speed stays steady.

items.t: Near Earth, falling speeds up by about 9.8 metres per second every second.
items.d: From rest: about 9.8 metres per second after 1 second, and about 19.6 after 2 seconds.

items.t: With no air resistance, a 45 degree angle sends a ball the farthest.
items.d: A steeper angle wastes forward speed. A flatter angle hits the ground too soon.

items.t: With no air in the way, how far and how high a ball goes does not depend on its weight.
items.d: Same starting speed and angle: a light ball and a heavy ball would follow the same path.

items.t: A dropped ball and a ball thrown sideways from the same height land together.
items.d: No air, and the sideways throw starts level. Sideways speed does not change the fall time.

items.t: Air resistance always pushes against the direction something is moving.
items.d: This push is called drag. Run or ride a bike and you feel it as wind on your face.

items.t: At high speeds, doubling your speed makes air drag about four times bigger.
items.d: Drag then grows with speed times speed. Two times two is four, so the push is four times as large.

items.t: A skydiver falls faster until air drag balances their weight.
items.d: Speed then stops rising. That top speed, terminal velocity, can be roughly 70 metres per second (250 km/h).

items.t: Pushing against air drag can take about 5 percent of a top sprinter's energy.
items.d: It is a small slice of the total, but in a short race that slice still counts.

items.t: A spinning ice skater goes faster by pulling arms and legs in close.
items.d: Angular momentum stays the same. A tighter body must spin faster to keep it.

items.t: A dimpled golf ball flies farther than a smooth one.
items.d: Dimples stir the air so it stays with the ball longer, and that makes drag smaller.

items.t: Divers press their hands together to make a rip entry with a tiny splash.
items.d: Clasped palms open an air pocket that pulls the splash down under the water.

items.t: Some racing swimsuits were designed to copy shark skin to help cut drag in the water.
items.d: The fabric has a rough pattern like a shark's skin. It was meant to reduce drag.

items.t: A curveball is slower than a fastball, about 105 to 129 kilometres per hour.
items.d: That is about 65 to 80 miles per hour, a usual range from college level upward.

items.t: In 1949, wind tunnel tests showed that a curveball really does curve.
items.d: The bend is not just an illusion. Air moving past the spinning ball pushes it off line.

items.t: A tennis ball dropped from 254 centimetres should bounce 135 to 147 centimetres.
items.d: The drop is onto concrete. It cannot bounce back to 254, because the hit wastes some energy.

items.t: Clap skates hinge, so the blade stays down on the ice as the heel lifts.
items.d: The heel detaches for part of each push, by a spring, and the glide lasts longer.

items.t: Cricket bowlers shine one side of the ball so it will swing in the air.
items.d: One shiny side and one rougher side let the air nudge the ball sideways.

items.t: A cricket ball's raised seam can make the ball move in the air or off the pitch.
items.d: Bowlers aim that stitched ridge so the air or the bounce changes the path.

items.t: A basketball bounces because it squashes on the floor, then springs back.
items.d: Its rubber bladder holds the air inside and gives the ball its spring.

items.t: In a Fosbury flop, the jumper's balance point can pass underneath the bar.
items.d: The body arches backward over the bar, so the jumper clears it while the middle stays lower.

items.t: In 1986 the men's javelin was redesigned to turn downward and land point first.
items.d: The balance point moved 4 centimetres forward, cutting flight distance by about 10 percent.

items.t: Shot putters release the shot at an angle a little under 45 degrees.
items.d: With no air, 45 degrees would go farthest. The shot is sent off a little flatter.

items.t: Some shot putters spin like a discus thrower to build turning power.
items.d: They use that rotational momentum to power the throw.

items.t: Hammer throwers usually make three or four spins, speeding the ball each time.
items.d: Now and then a thrower uses five spins. Each turn makes the hammer move faster.

items.t: The faster a discus spins, the steadier it is while it flies.
items.d: A quick spin keeps the discus steady, like a spinning top, so it holds its angle.

items.t: Discus throwers travel farthest when they throw into a moderate headwind.
items.d: A gentle wind toward the thrower gives a longer flight than still air does.

items.t: A returning boomerang is a spinning wing, and the spin bends its path back to you.
items.d: The spinning wing slowly tilts as it flies, so its path bends into a wide curve.

items.t: During a boomerang's spin, the upper arm moves faster and makes more lift.
items.d: That arm meets the air at a higher speed on the top half of each turn.

items.t: Most Aboriginal hunting boomerangs did not return. They were meant to fly straight.
items.d: Those throws usually went about 40 to 90 metres in a straight line.

items.t: Pole vaulters turn the energy of their run into energy stored in a bent pole.
items.d: Moving energy from the run becomes stored energy in the bent, springy pole.

items.t: At about 32 kilometres per hour on the flat, air drag takes about three quarters of the effort.
items.d: For a rider plus bike of about 90 kilograms, pushing the air aside is the big share of the work.

items.t: Power to overcome a bike's air drag grows with speed times speed times speed.
items.d: Double the speed and that power is about 8 times larger, because 2 x 2 x 2 = 8.

items.t: Cycle racers share the lead, then drop back to rest in the shelter of others.
items.d: The front rider breaks the wind. Behind them, the air drag is smaller, so legs can recover.

items.t: A clean, oiled bicycle chain can deliver up to 99 percent of pedal energy to the wheels.
items.d: Very little energy is wasted in the chain. Almost all of your push reaches the tyres.

items.t: At the same power, cycling a distance uses about one third the energy of walking.
items.d: You are faster on a bike, so that same power is used for less time over the same distance.

items.t: The tuck, where a diver curls into a tight ball, is the easiest shape for spin.
items.d: With arms and legs pulled in, the diver can control the rotation more easily.

items.t: A diver reaches the water at about 55 kilometres per hour from a 10 metre platform.
items.d: From 6 metres up, the speed at the water is lower, about 40 kilometres per hour.

items.t: A flying disc keeps its aim in the air because spinning steadies it.
items.d: Spin keeps the disc steady, like a spinning top. That stops it tumbling and lets it travel farther.

items.t: A flying disc is shaped like a wing, so the air lifts it and drag is lower.
items.d: The curved cross-section is an airfoil, the same kind of shape a plane wing uses.

items.t: Fuzzy felt on a tennis ball cuts drag by keeping the air close to the ball longer.
items.d: When the air stays attached a bit longer, the backward pull on the ball gets smaller.

items.t: Centripetal means center-seeking. It comes from Latin words for center and to seek.
items.d: Anything moving in a circle needs a center-seeking pull or push.

items.t: Centripetal force always points toward the middle of the circle an object is moving around.
items.d: Swing a toy on a string and the string pulls it toward your hand.

items.t: Gravity is the centripetal force that keeps planets and moons moving around in their orbits.
items.d: Earth's gravity keeps the Moon circling us instead of flying off.

items.t: When you whirl a ball on a string, the string's tension pulls it toward the middle.
items.d: If released, the ball starts moving straight in the direction it was going.

items.t: At the same circle size, going twice as fast needs four times as much inward force.
items.d: The inward force depends on speed squared: 2 times the speed needs 4 times the force.

items.t: On a flat road with no grip, a car would slide straight on instead of turning around a curve.
items.d: This is why tires need grip, especially on a wet road.

items.t: Because Earth spins, it bulges a little at the equator and is slightly flattened at the poles.
items.d: So Earth is not a perfect ball, it is a bit squashed.

items.t: Centrifuges use fast spinning to separate different substances in science and industry.
items.d: Denser parts move outward more than less dense parts.

items.t: A spinning object keeps spinning the same way unless something outside twists it.
items.d: This is called conservation of angular momentum.

items.t: A figure skater spins faster when she pulls her arms and legs in close.
items.d: Pulling her arms and legs inward makes her spin speed increase.

items.t: The Moon's pull on the tides is slowly slowing Earth's spin, by about 65.7 nanoseconds a day.
items.d: A nanosecond is one billionth of a second, so days barely change.

items.t: Hurricanes form spirals, and neutron stars spin very fast. Angular momentum helps explain both.
items.d: A star that shrinks spins faster, like a skater pulling in her arms.

items.t: Leon Foucault named the gyroscope in 1852 while using it to show that Earth rotates.
items.d: He used the spinning wheel to show that Earth turns.

items.t: A gyrocompass uses a spinning wheel to find true north by sensing Earth's rotation.
items.d: It finds north with a spinning wheel instead of a magnet.

items.t: The Russian space station Mir used spinning flywheels called gyrodynes to help steer.
items.d: Spinning wheels inside the station could turn it without any rocket fuel.

items.t: A small gyroscope fitted in a bicycle wheel has been sold as an alternative to training wheels.
items.d: The spinning gyroscope resists changes to the wheel's tilt, helping the bicycle balance.

items.t: When Hubble turns, its gyro wheel resists and its axis tilts. That shows how fast Hubble is turning.
items.d: The tilt gives the telescope's computer a measurement of its turning.

items.t: To point in every direction, a spacecraft needs three reaction wheels set at right angles to each other.
items.d: Think of the three edges meeting at the corner of a box.

items.t: A spinning object tends to keep its axis steady. This is called gyroscopic inertia.
items.d: A spinning bicycle wheel is hard to tilt when you hold it by the axle.

items.t: NASA says gyroscopes are simple devices that seem to defy gravity.
items.d: A spinning gyroscope can balance in ways a still one never could.

items.t: Gyroscopes help the International Space Station and the Hubble Space Telescope stay on course.
items.d: They tell the spacecraft which way it is facing.

items.t: In 1864 Antonin Prandtl proposed a centrifuge to separate cream from milk. A working one was shown in 1875.
items.d: The spinning flings the heavier milk outward and leaves cream near the middle.

items.t: Human centrifuges are giant spinners that test how pilots and astronauts cope with strong forces.
items.d: The rider sits at the end of a long arm that whirls around.

items.t: Washing machines work as centrifuges. They spin fast to throw extra water out of clothes.
items.d: Water goes through the tiny holes in the drum, but the clothes stay inside.

items.t: Some swimming pools have small spinners that fling the water out of wet swimsuits.
items.d: It is the same idea as the spin cycle in a washing machine.

items.t: A teardrop-shaped loop gives riders gentler g-forces than a perfect circle would.
items.d: The wide curve at the bottom makes the turn smoother for riders.

items.t: In 1966 the Gemini 11 crew spun their capsule on a tether to make a tiny bit of artificial gravity.
items.d: It was only about 0.00015 g, far too small for the astronauts to feel.

items.t: The smaller a spinning spacecraft is, the faster it must turn to make artificial gravity.
items.d: A big wheel can make the same gravity with a slow spin.

items.t: In the Rotor ride the floor drops away, but riders stay stuck to the wall.
items.d: The spinning wall keeps pressing inward on them.

items.t: As a Rotor ride slows down, gravity takes over and riders slide slowly down the wall.
items.d: The inward push gets weaker as the spin slows.

items.t: Most modern washing machines spin at 1,000 to 1,600 turns every minute.
items.d: That is about 17 to 27 turns every second.

items.t: Faster spin speeds and bigger drums make more g-force, so more water leaves the clothes.
items.d: Clothes come out damp rather than dripping.

items.t: Many washing machines have rings filled with liquid to keep the drum balanced as it spins.
items.d: An uneven load can make the drum shake without them.

items.t: At the equator, Earth's spin carries you around at about 1,675 km per hour.
items.d: You move steadily with Earth, so you do not notice this speed directly.

items.t: At the North and South Poles, Earth's spinning speed is almost zero.
items.d: Standing on a pole, you would just slowly turn in place once a day.

items.t: Earth rotates toward the east. Seen from above the North Pole, it turns counterclockwise.
items.d: That is why the Sun rises in the east.

items.t: Earth's axis is tilted by about 23.4 degrees.
items.d: It is like a spinning top that leans a little to one side.

items.t: Hurricanes spin counterclockwise north of the equator and clockwise south of it.
items.d: Earth's spin causes a Coriolis effect that helps set their direction of spin.

items.t: On a spinning carousel, a ball thrown straight looks like it curves to someone riding.
items.d: To someone standing outside, the ball goes straight.

items.t: Spinning tops are among the oldest known toys and have been found on every inhabited continent.
items.d: Children have played with tops for thousands of years.

items.t: Clay spinning tops made in Mesopotamia are about 5,000 years old.
items.d: Mesopotamia was an ancient land, mostly in what is now Iraq.

items.t: A tilted spinning top slowly swings its axis around in a circle. This is called precession.
items.d: Watch the top of a toy top draw a slow circle as it spins.

items.t: A spinning top stays balanced on its tip thanks to the gyroscopic effect.
items.d: A top that is not spinning falls over at once.

items.t: A pulsar is a spinning neutron star that sends out beams, like a lighthouse in space.
items.d: We see a flash each time a beam sweeps past Earth.

items.t: The fastest known pulsar spins about 716 times every second.
items.d: That is 716 spins in the time it takes to say one second.

items.t: Jocelyn Bell spotted the first pulsar in 1967 while studying radio telescope data.
items.d: At first the pulses looked so regular that people wondered what made them.

items.t: The first pulsar signal pulsed evenly about every 1.337 seconds.
items.d: That is a little slower than a typical heartbeat.

items.t: Jupiter spins once in slightly less than ten hours, faster than any other planet.
items.d: A day on Jupiter is less than half an Earth day.

items.t: Jupiter's fast spin makes it bulge. Its equatorial radius is about 7% longer than its polar radius.
items.d: Fast spinning squashes the planet, like Earth but much more.

items.t: Jupiter's Great Red Spot is a storm that turns counterclockwise about once every six days.
items.d: It is a giant swirling storm on the planet.

items.t: The word aerodynamics comes from 'aero', which means air, and 'dynamic', which means motion.
items.d: So aerodynamics is the study of how air moves around things.

items.t: A glider can fly without an engine.
items.d: They ride on the air instead of pushing through it with power.

items.t: On a normal airplane, engines mostly fight drag, while the wings make most of the lift.
items.d: Engines push the plane forward so the wings can keep making lift.

items.t: When the four forces on a plane are balanced, it cruises along at a steady speed.
items.d: The forces are lift, weight, thrust and drag.

items.t: A plane gets lighter during a flight because it burns fuel.
items.d: Its weight keeps changing all the way from takeoff to landing.

items.t: Drag is the push of air against an aircraft, and it acts against the way the aircraft moves.
items.d: You feel drag when you stick your hand out of a moving car window.

items.t: With no air or other fluid, there is no drag.
items.d: That is why drag matters for planes but not for things moving in empty space.

items.t: A smooth, waxed surface makes less skin friction drag than a rough one.
items.d: Smooth surfaces let air slip past more easily.

items.t: To get lift, there must be motion between the object and the air. No motion, no lift.
items.d: A kite hangs limp in still air but lifts when the wind blows.

items.t: The Wright brothers built a wind tunnel from a fan pushing air through a long wooden box.
items.d: They tested small wing shapes inside it.

items.t: The Wrights' 1901 glider made only about a third of the lift they expected, so they built a wind tunnel.
items.d: They wanted to find out why their numbers were wrong.

items.t: A spinning ball curves because the air next to its surface is dragged around with the spin.
items.d: That turns the airflow and pushes the ball sideways.

items.t: Helicopters can take off and land without a runway.
items.d: That helps them reach places planes cannot.

items.t: An airplane must fly fast to get air over its wings. A helicopter spins its blades instead.
items.d: So a helicopter can lift off without moving forward.

items.t: The Wrights' first powered flight, in 1903, lasted 12 seconds and went about 37 metres.
items.d: It reached about 11 km per hour.

items.t: A paper airplane glides using the height and push it gets from the person who throws it.
items.d: The energy for its flight comes from your arm.

items.t: Paper airplanes get lift by tilting their flat wings up a little against the air.
items.d: That tilt is called the angle of attack.

items.t: On the downstroke, a bird's wing makes both lift and forward push.
items.d: On the upstroke it partly folds to cut resistance.

items.t: Kites are heavier than air. They fly because of forces from the wind, not because of buoyancy.
items.d: Balloons are different. They float on buoyancy.

items.t: Your voice starts with two small folds in your throat that open and close very fast, letting out puffs of air.
items.d: Those puffs of air make sound waves that travel out of your mouth.

items.t: When you whisper, your vocal folds do not vibrate. The rushing air makes a noisy hiss instead.
items.d: Try humming, then whispering. Put your fingers on your throat to feel the difference.

items.t: Your muscles cannot shake your vocal folds directly. They vibrate far too fast for muscles to keep up.
items.d: The air flowing past the folds makes them vibrate, not a muscle twitch.

items.t: Your mouth and throat boost some sound frequencies more than others. These boosts are called formants.
items.d: Changing your mouth shape changes the sound, even when your pitch stays the same.

items.t: Vowels like 'ee' and 'ah' sound different mainly because of the first two formants made by your mouth shape.
items.d: Say 'ee' then 'ah' slowly and feel your tongue and lips move.

items.t: How high or low a voice sounds depends on the length, size and tension of the vocal folds.
items.d: These features affect how fast the folds vibrate.

items.t: Vocal folds vibrate about 125 times a second in a grown man, 210 in a grown woman and over 300 in children.
items.d: That means a child's vocal folds can vibrate more than 300 times in one second.

items.t: Children have higher voices because their vocal folds are much shorter than those of adults.
items.d: Shorter vocal folds can vibrate faster, which makes a higher sound.

items.t: Vocal folds are about 6 to 8 mm long at birth. By the teen years they are about 8 to 16 mm.
items.d: As the folds grow longer, the voice usually gets lower.

items.t: Harmonics are tones whose frequencies are whole-number multiples of the lowest tone, called the fundamental.
items.d: If the lowest tone vibrates 100 times a second, the next ones are 200, 300 and 400.

items.t: The second harmonic sounds exactly one octave higher than the fundamental.
items.d: An octave is the jump between two notes with the same name, like one C to the next C.

items.t: An instrument's tone colour, called timbre, mostly depends on how strong each of its harmonics is.
items.d: That is why a flute and a trumpet sound different even on the very same note.

items.t: A clarinet has weaker even-numbered harmonics than a saxophone, so they sound different.
items.d: A saxophone's tube is cone-shaped.

items.t: Your brain can hear a note's pitch even if its lowest harmonic is missing. This is the missing fundamental.
items.d: Your brain fills in the pitch from the other harmonics.

items.t: A piano makes sound when a key makes a felt-covered hammer hit a string.
items.d: The hammer bounces back right away so the string can ring freely.

items.t: Piano string vibrations pass through a bridge to a big wooden soundboard, which makes them louder.
items.d: The soundboard pushes on lots of air, like a big wooden loudspeaker.

items.t: Most piano notes have three strings struck together. The lowest bass notes have only one or two.
items.d: Thick, heavy bass strings are strong enough to make a loud sound alone.

items.t: When you let go of a piano key, a damper presses on the string and stops the sound.
items.d: The right pedal lifts all the dampers so notes keep ringing.

items.t: A modern piano has 88 black and white keys.
items.d: That is 52 white keys and 36 black keys.

items.t: A guitar string is stretched between two fixed points. When it vibrates, it makes sound.
items.d: Plucking a string moves it back and forth many times each second.

items.t: On an acoustic guitar the hollow wooden body makes the quiet string sound much louder.
items.d: Without the body, a plucked string would be very quiet.

items.t: Pressing a guitar string against a fret makes the string shorter, so the note sounds higher.
items.d: A shorter vibrating string usually vibrates faster, which makes a higher note.

items.t: An electric guitar's pickups turn string vibrations into electric signals. An amplifier makes them louder.
items.d: The solid body does not need to be hollow, because the amplifier does the loud part.

items.t: A bass guitar is usually tuned E, A, D, G, an octave below the bottom four strings of a six-string guitar.
items.d: Longer, thicker strings make lower sounds.

items.t: A violinist draws a bow across a string. The string vibrates and makes a long, steady sound.
items.d: Bowing can keep the note going.

items.t: Bow hair is rubbed with rosin so it grips. Friction between hair and string makes the string vibrate.
items.d: Without rosin, the bow would slide over the string and stay quiet.

items.t: The four violin strings are tuned a perfect fifth apart: G, D, A and E.
items.d: Going from one string to the next goes up by the same musical step.

items.t: A violin's bridge carries the strings' vibrations into the hollow wooden body.
items.d: Inside, a small wooden soundpost helps shape how the body vibrates.

items.t: A flute makes sound when a stream of air across a hole makes the air inside the tube vibrate.
items.d: You can try this by blowing gently across the top of an empty bottle.

items.t: Opening and closing a flute's finger holes changes the length of its vibrating air. That changes the note.
items.d: A shorter air column gives a higher note.

items.t: Recorders and tin whistles are called fipple flutes. A duct sends air onto a sharp edge.
items.d: The duct does the job that a flute player's lips do.

items.t: Blowing harder on a flute can make it jump to a higher harmonic. This is called overblowing.
items.d: The same tube can play higher notes without changing its length.

items.t: Flutes with hand-bored holes from the Stone Age are among the oldest known musical instruments.
items.d: People were making music with tubes and holes long before cities existed.

items.t: A whistle makes a nearly pure tone, a clean note with very few extra harmonics.
items.d: A whistle's sound comes from a stream of air hitting a sharp edge.

items.t: A drum is a stretched skin, called a drumhead, over a shell. Hitting the skin makes it vibrate and make sound.
items.d: The drumhead affects how a drum sounds more than any other part.

items.t: Tightening a drumhead makes the drum's pitch higher.
items.d: A tight skin springs back faster, so it vibrates faster.

items.t: A drum with a larger shell diameter usually has a lower pitch.
items.d: A big bass drum booms low, while a small drum often sounds higher.

items.t: The wooden or metal shell of a drum vibrates with the skin and can make the sound louder.
items.d: A drum without a shell would sound much thinner and quieter.

items.t: A snare drum has wires stretched across one or both heads. They buzz when the drum is hit.
items.d: That buzz gives a snare drum its crisp, rattling sound.

items.t: Timpani are big orchestra drums. A foot pedal lets players quickly change them to exact notes.
items.d: Pressing the pedal tightens the skin, which raises the pitch.

items.t: Symphony orchestras usually tune to the note A at 440 vibrations per second.
items.d: Players tune their instruments to this shared reference.

items.t: Equal temperament, common in Western music, splits an octave into twelve equal musical steps.
items.d: Each step changes frequency by the same ratio.

items.t: Two almost-matching notes make a wobbling sound called beats. The beats slow down as the notes get closer.
items.d: Tuners listen for the beats to stop. Then the notes match.

items.t: A tuning fork is a U-shaped bar of springy metal, usually steel, with two prongs.
items.d: When you hit it, the prongs move back and forth and make a clear sound.

items.t: A tuning fork makes a very pure tone, mostly at just one frequency.
items.d: That is why musicians use one as a clean reference note.

items.t: A tuning fork's pitch depends on the length and mass of its prongs.
items.d: Longer prongs vibrate slower, so they make a lower note.

items.t: A brass player's buzzing lips make the air inside the instrument's tube vibrate.
items.d: The tube makes the buzz louder and shapes it into a musical note.

items.t: Pressing a trumpet valve sends air through extra tubing. The tube gets longer and the note gets lower.
items.d: A longer tube means a lower note, just like a longer organ pipe.

items.t: Each organ pipe plays only one pitch, so a pipe organ needs a lot of pipes.
items.d: Longer pipes sound lower, and shorter pipes sound higher.

items.t: An organ can hold a note as long as the key is pressed, because air keeps flowing through the pipes.
items.d: A piano note fades away, but an organ note can last as long as you hold it.

items.t: Clarinets and saxophones use one reed. Oboes use two reeds that vibrate against each other.
items.d: Most reeds are cut from a tall, tough cane plant.

items.t: Every bar of a xylophone is tuned to a note of a musical scale.
items.d: Shorter bars sound higher and longer bars sound lower.

items.t: A loudspeaker has a coil that moves back and forth when an electric signal flows through it.
items.d: A permanent magnet makes the strong magnetic field the coil moves in.

items.t: A speaker's light cone is attached to the coil. As the coil moves, the cone pushes air and makes sound waves.
items.d: If you touch a loud speaker lightly, you can feel the cone shaking.

items.t: A woofer plays low sounds and a tweeter plays high ones. A crossover sends each sound to the right one.
items.d: Big drivers handle low sounds well. Small drivers handle high sounds well.

items.t: Headphones began because telephone operators needed their hands free.
items.d: Early headsets let them take calls and work at the same time.

items.t: Active noise-cancelling headphones can reduce outside noise by 20 decibels or more.
items.d: They play a sound wave that cancels some of the noise.

items.t: American physicist Wallace Sabine did the first modern scientific study of how sound behaves in rooms.
items.d: He used what he learned to help design Symphony Hall in Boston.

items.t: Sound bouncing around a room makes standing waves and natural resonances.
items.d: Singing in a small bathroom can make some notes sound extra loud.

items.t: Diffusers scatter sound in many directions, which can make a room sound better.
items.d: Concert halls often have bumpy walls for this reason.

items.t: Reverberation time is how long a sound takes to fade by 60 decibels.
items.d: A big stone church has a long reverberation time. A carpeted bedroom has a short one.

items.t: Rooms for speech need a short reverberation time so words stay clear.
items.d: Too much echo mixes the words together, so they are hard to understand.

items.t: Sound reflections less than about 50 milliseconds apart blend into reverberation, not echoes.
items.d: A true echo needs a longer gap, like shouting at a far-away wall.

items.t: Light is one small slice of a huge wave family called the electromagnetic spectrum.
items.d: Your eyes can only see the visible slice. Radio, X-rays and more are all around, hidden from sight.

items.t: The electromagnetic spectrum runs from very long radio waves to very short gamma rays.
items.d: Radio waves are the longest in the family, and gamma rays are the shortest.

items.t: Tuning a radio and sending a text both use electromagnetic waves.
items.d: Your phone and a radio talk to the world through waves you cannot see.

items.t: The Sun sends out energy across the whole electromagnetic spectrum.
items.d: Sunlight is only the part we can see. The rest is invisible.

items.t: In 1932, Karl Jansky showed that stars and other things in space give off radio waves.
items.d: So space is not silent. Telescopes can listen to it with radio dishes.

items.t: Radio telescope dishes can be full of tiny holes, because long radio waves pass over the holes.
items.d: The holes make the dish lighter, but it still catches the waves.

items.t: Microwave ovens heat food by making water and fat molecules in it spin.
items.d: That spinning makes the food warm, like rubbing your hands together.

items.t: Some microwaves can travel through clouds, dust, smoke, snow and rain.
items.d: This is why satellites can use them to peek at Earth in bad weather.

items.t: A satellite can measure sea height by timing how long a microwave pulse takes to bounce back.
items.d: Longer trip means the sea is farther below the satellite.

items.t: The cosmic microwave background is faint microwave energy that fills the whole universe.
items.d: It was found by accident in 1965 and is a clue to how the universe began.

items.t: You cannot see infrared light, but you can feel it as heat.
items.d: Hold your hand near a warm lamp and you feel infrared.

items.t: Infrared light passes through thick clouds of space dust better than visible light does.
items.d: That lets infrared telescopes see things hidden from normal telescopes.

items.t: X-rays have tiny wavelengths, only about 0.03 to 3 nanometres long.
items.d: A nanometre is a billionth of a metre, far smaller than a speck of dust.

items.t: Bones show up on X-ray pictures because dense bone soaks up more X-rays than skin does.
items.d: That is why bones look bright in an X-ray picture.

items.t: X-ray telescopes use mirrors set at very shallow angles to focus X-rays.
items.d: The rays skim the mirror like a stone skipping on water.

items.t: UV rays can reach you on cloudy and cool days, not just hot sunny ones.
items.d: Sun protection is a good idea even when the sky is gray.

items.t: A shadow shorter than you are means the sun's UV rays are stronger.
items.d: Check your shadow on a sunny day to see.

items.t: Most TV remotes send tiny pulses of infrared light that your eyes cannot see.
items.d: A digital camera can often show the flashing light from a remote.

items.t: Wi-Fi lets nearby devices share data using radio waves.
items.d: Most Wi-Fi uses radio bands of about 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz.

items.t: The metal mesh in a microwave door keeps microwaves inside but lets you see in.
items.d: The tiny holes are too small for the waves, but light slips through.

items.t: All electromagnetic waves travel at the speed of light in empty space.
items.d: That is about 300,000 km per second.

items.t: A mirage is a real optical effect, not a trick of the mind.
items.d: A camera can photograph a mirage.

items.t: On a hot, sunny day, a road may seem to have puddles that are not there.
items.d: Bent light creates the watery-looking image.

items.t: A 22-degree halo is a large ring around the Sun or Moon.
items.d: Tiny ice crystals in the air make the ring.

items.t: Halos form when light passes through tiny ice crystals high in the air.
items.d: These crystals are often inside thin cirrus clouds.

items.t: Ice crystals can bend and bounce light like tiny prisms and mirrors.
items.d: This helps create bright halos in the sky.

items.t: Ice crystals can split light into rainbow-like colours.
items.d: The splitting of light into colours is called dispersion.

items.t: A light pillar is a vertical column of light near the Sun.
items.d: It may appear around sunrise or sunset.

items.t: Auroras begin with charged particles from the Sun.
items.d: The particles collide with atoms in Earth's atmosphere.

items.t: Auroras can shine in green, red and purple.
items.d: Different gases and conditions produce different colours.

items.t: Auroras glow when collisions excite oxygen and nitrogen in the air.
items.d: The excited gases release colourful light.

items.t: Auroras can form shapes like curtains, rays and spirals.
items.d: Their glowing patterns can shift across the sky.

items.t: Bioluminescence is light made and released by a living thing.
items.d: Some ocean animals make their own glow.

items.t: Bioluminescence comes from a chemical reaction inside a living thing.
items.d: A substance called luciferin reacts with an enzyme.

items.t: Some squid glow to match light coming from above.
items.d: This can hide their shadow from animals looking up from below.

items.t: Under ultraviolet light, many substances glow with visible colours.
items.d: This effect is called fluorescence.

items.t: Highlighter ink is often fluorescent.
items.d: Many highlighters contain a glowing chemical called pyranine.

items.t: Many calcite minerals glow under ultraviolet light.
items.d: This glow is fluorescence.

items.t: Fluorescent light usually has less energy than the light the material absorbed.
items.d: It also usually has a longer wavelength.

items.t: Flying squirrels can glow pink under ultraviolet light.
items.d: This surprising fluorescence was noticed by chance in 2019.

items.t: Glow-in-the-dark toys, stickers and paints use phosphorescence.
items.d: They keep shining after the room becomes dark.

items.t: Glow sticks shine by chemiluminescence, not phosphorescence.
items.d: Their light comes from a chemical reaction.

items.t: In a laser, one passing photon can trigger the release of an identical photon.
items.d: This process is called stimulated emission.

items.t: Dennis Gabor invented holography in 1948.
items.d: He was trying to improve images from an electron microscope.

items.t: TV remote controls use infrared LEDs to send signals.
items.d: Infrared light cannot be seen by human eyes.

items.t: Blue LEDs made practical white LED lights possible.
items.d: Their invention was honoured by the 2014 Nobel Prize in Physics.

items.t: Stars twinkle because their light passes through moving layers of air.
items.d: The turbulent atmosphere bends the starlight in changing ways.

items.t: Energy is never used up. It only changes from one form to another.
items.d: When you eat lunch and then run, food energy turns into motion and heat.

items.t: In an isolated system, the total amount of energy always stays the same.
items.d: Energy can change form inside it, but the total does not change.

items.t: A machine that gives out energy with nothing put in can never exist.
items.d: Such a perpetual-motion machine would break the law of energy conservation.

items.t: Mathematician Emmy Noether showed energy conservation comes from physics rules staying the same over time.
items.d: The rules of physics work the same today as they did yesterday.

items.t: A German doctor, Julius Robert von Mayer, stated the modern idea of energy conservation in 1842.
items.d: Big ideas in physics can come from people with other jobs, like doctors.

items.t: The watt is named after James Watt, the Scottish inventor who improved the steam engine in 1776.
items.d: A watt measures power, how fast energy is used.

items.t: One watt means one joule of energy is used every second.
items.d: A 60 W bulb uses 60 joules of energy every second.

items.t: A laser pointer gives out about 5 milliwatts of light power.
items.d: That is only 0.005 watts, a tiny amount of power.

items.t: A small electric heater can use about 1 kilowatt of power.
items.d: 1 kilowatt is 1,000 watts, the same as ten 100 W bulbs.

items.t: A 100 W bulb left on for one hour uses 0.1 kilowatt-hour of energy.
items.d: Ten hours of that bulb would use 1 kilowatt-hour.

items.t: One kilowatt-hour is 3,600,000 joules of energy.
items.d: 1,000 watts for 3,600 seconds (one hour) is 1,000 x 3,600 = 3,600,000.

items.t: A 100 kg person climbing a 3 m ladder in 5 seconds works at roughly 600 watts.
items.d: Climbing the same ladder faster takes more power.

items.t: One joule is the work done when a force of one newton moves something one metre in its direction.
items.d: A newton is about the weight of a small apple.

items.t: An adult needs about 1,600 to 3,000 food Calories of energy every day.
items.d: Food is fuel for your body. Very active people need more.

items.t: In a power station, a turbo generator turns energy from pressurized steam into electricity.
items.d: Moving steam spins the turbine, and the spinning makes electricity.

items.t: Einstein showed that mass and energy are related.
items.d: One kilogram of mass has an energy equivalent of about 90 million billion joules.

items.t: A swinging pendulum with no friction keeps swapping energy between stored and moving forms.
items.d: At the top of the swing it is stored. At the bottom it moves fastest.

items.t: Most roller coaster trains are pulled up a lift hill by a chain or cable, then let go.
items.d: The train starts its fast ride from the highest point.

items.t: On a roller coaster, energy stored by climbing the lift hill turns into motion on the way down.
items.d: Higher at the start means more energy to use for the whole ride.

items.t: Each hill on a coaster is usually lower than the one before it.
items.d: Friction and air drag turn some mechanical energy into heat, so the train cannot climb as high.

items.t: A roller coaster usually stops on a brake run, where motion energy becomes heat.
items.d: Brakes can get warm, like your hands when you rub them together.

items.t: Some roller coasters skip the lift hill and use a flywheel or linear motor to launch.
items.d: The launch system gives the train its starting speed.

items.t: Ordinary roller coaster trains have no engine. Gravity does the work after the first lift.
items.d: The chain does the climbing work, then gravity pulls the train around.

items.t: The ancestors of roller coasters were ice slides called Russian Mountains, from the 1600s.
items.d: People slid down tall ice hills in what is now Saint Petersburg, Russia.

items.t: An early track-based roller coaster, Thompson's Switchback Railway, opened at Coney Island in 1884.
items.d: It was a long way from today's tall, fast coasters.

items.t: An old-style filament bulb turns less than 5% of its energy into visible light. The rest is heat.
items.d: That is why old-style bulbs become hot.

items.t: Old-style filament bulbs usually last only 1,000 to 2,000 hours.
items.d: Left on all the time, that is only about 6 to 12 weeks.

items.t: White LED bulbs can last an estimated 35,000 to 50,000 hours.
items.d: Used 3 hours a day, 35,000 hours is more than 30 years.

items.t: Edison's successful lamp test on 22 October 1879 lasted 13.5 hours.
items.d: It was an early test of Edison's lamp design.

items.t: Alessandro Volta built the first electrochemical battery, the voltaic pile, in 1800.
items.d: Batteries have been storing energy for more than 200 years.

items.t: Inventor Joseph Swan's house, Underhill, was the first in the world lit by a lightbulb.
items.d: Electric light was once so new that one house made history.

items.t: The 2014 Nobel Prize in Physics honoured the inventors of the blue LED.
items.d: Blue LEDs made bright white LED lights possible.

items.t: In an LED, electrons give up energy as tiny packets of light called photons.
items.d: The light comes from inside a tiny piece of semiconductor.

items.t: An electric motor turns electrical energy into motion.
items.d: Fans, washing machines and electric cars all use motors.

items.t: Elastic energy is stored when something is squashed, stretched or bent.
items.d: A stretched rubber band or a squashed spring is storing energy.

items.t: When a stretched or squashed object springs back, its stored energy can become motion and sound.
items.d: Release a stretched rubber band and it springs back with a twang.

items.t: An ideal spring stores four times more energy when you stretch it twice as far.
items.d: Stretch it 2 cm and then 4 cm, and the 4 cm stretch stores 4 times as much.

items.t: A regenerative brake uses an electric motor as a generator to catch energy that might become heat.
items.d: The slowing train or car helps make electricity.

items.t: Energy caught by regenerative braking can be stored in a battery, capacitors or a spinning flywheel.
items.d: The saved energy can help the vehicle speed up again.

items.t: On the Kiruna to Narvik line, downhill trains make more electricity than the railway uses.
items.d: Their regenerative brakes act like generators.

items.t: The joule, a unit of energy, is named after English physicist James Prescott Joule.
items.d: He lived from 1818 to 1889.

items.t: One joule is about the energy needed to lift an apple one metre.
items.d: Lifting it just one metre, about up to your chest, takes about one joule.

items.t: One calorie equals about 4.184 joules.
items.d: So 10 calories is about 41.84 joules.

items.t: Food labels in most countries give energy in kilojoules.
items.d: One kilojoule is 1,000 joules.

items.t: For small swings in one place, a pendulum's swing time depends on its length, not its mass.
items.d: A short pendulum swings faster than a long one.

items.t: Christiaan Huygens built the first pendulum clock in 1656, a big step toward accurate clocks.
items.d: Older clocks could be wrong by 15 minutes a day. His was off by about 15 seconds a day.

items.t: A clock pendulum needs a small push each swing to replace the energy lost to friction.
items.d: Without the little pushes, the pendulum would slowly stop.

items.t: A generator turns motion energy into electrical energy.
items.d: Wind, water or steam can spin a generator.

items.t: Hydropower uses moving water as fuel, but the water is not used up.
items.d: After passing through the plant, the water returns to the water cycle.

items.t: Moving water can push turbine blades and make them turn.
items.d: It works a bit like wind spinning a pinwheel.

items.t: A spinning water turbine drives a generator, which makes electricity.
items.d: The turbine provides motion, and the generator changes that motion into electricity.

items.t: More flowing water can help a hydropower plant make more electricity.
items.d: Water falling from a greater height can also provide more power.

items.t: Rain and snow help refill the water supplies used for hydropower.
items.d: This happens through Earth's repeating water cycle.

items.t: Flowing water has kinetic energy, which means energy of motion.
items.d: Hydropower plants capture some of this moving energy.

items.t: Hydropower was one of the first energy sources used to make electricity.
items.d: People learned to use moving water for electrical power long ago.

items.t: A penstock is a large pipe that carries water toward a hydro turbine.
items.d: The rushing water leaves the pipe and pushes the turbine blades.

items.t: Pumped-storage plants pump water uphill to store energy.
items.d: They release the water to make electricity when more power is needed.

items.t: Most U.S. hydropower plants use a dam and reservoir to hold water.
items.d: The stored water can later flow through equipment that makes electricity.

items.t: Geothermal energy is heat found inside Earth.
items.d: Geo means Earth, and thermal relates to heat.

items.t: Geothermal energy is renewable because Earth keeps producing heat.
items.d: Its power source is heat from inside our planet.

items.t: Some of Earth's inner heat comes from radioactive particles slowly breaking down.
items.d: This natural process releases heat deep inside the planet.

items.t: Rocks and water usually get hotter as you travel deeper into Earth.
items.d: Geothermal systems can use this underground heat.

items.t: People use geothermal heat for hot-spring bathing and for electricity.
items.d: The same kind of underground heat can serve different purposes.

items.t: Geothermal power plants can run day and night in any weather.
items.d: Their heat source is underground, so sunshine and wind are not required.

items.t: Geothermal heat has made electricity in the United States for over 60 years.
items.d: Power plants have used Earth's inner heat for many decades.

items.t: Steam turbines make most of the world's electricity.
items.d: Steam spins a turbine that helps drive a generator.

items.t: Many power plants burn fuel in a boiler to make hot water and steam.
items.d: The steam then spins a turbine.

items.t: A combustion gas turbine works somewhat like a jet engine.
items.d: It burns a gas or liquid fuel to produce power.

items.t: Nuclear power plants use fuel rods to produce steam.
items.d: The steam spins turbines used to make electricity.

items.t: Diesel-engine generators can use several kinds of fuel.
items.d: Petroleum diesel is one fuel they can use, but it is not the only one.

items.t: Nuclear fission splits atoms and releases energy.
items.d: A nuclear power plant uses the released energy as a source of heat.

items.t: Most nuclear power plants use uranium atoms as fuel.
items.d: Energy is released when uranium atoms split through fission.

items.t: Nuclear plants use a kind of uranium called U-235 as fuel.
items.d: U-235 atoms can split and release energy.

items.t: A nuclear reactor carefully controls its fission reaction.
items.d: The reaction is controlled to produce the amount of heat the plant needs.

items.t: A huge amount of energy holds the particles in an atom's nucleus together.
items.d: Nuclear energy comes from this tiny central part of an atom.

items.t: Coal is a black or brownish-black rock rich in carbon.
items.d: Its stored chemical energy can be released as heat when coal burns.

items.t: Coal is nonrenewable because it takes millions of years to form.
items.d: People use coal far faster than nature can replace it.

items.t: Coal stores energy from plants that lived hundreds of millions of years ago.
items.d: Many of those ancient plants grew in swampy forests.

items.t: Anthracite coal is about 86 to 97 percent carbon.
items.d: It generally has the highest heating value of the coal ranks.

items.t: Lignite is a moist, crumbly kind of coal with a low heating value.
items.d: Its high moisture helps explain why it provides less heat.

items.t: Natural gas formed from buried remains changed by heat and pressure.
items.d: The remains came from ancient plants and animals.

items.t: Methane is the largest part of natural gas.
items.d: Natural gas can contain other substances too, but methane is its main component.

items.t: One methane molecule has one carbon atom and four hydrogen atoms.
items.d: Its chemical formula is CH4.

items.t: Natural gas has no color, smell, or taste on its own.
items.d: Its familiar smell does not come from the gas itself.

items.t: Gas companies add a smelly chemical called mercaptan to natural gas.
items.d: The added odor makes leaking gas easier to notice.

items.t: Mercaptan gives natural gas a smell often compared to rotten eggs.
items.d: The smelly chemical added to the gas is harmless.

items.t: Crude oil is a fossil fuel formed from the remains of plants and animals.
items.d: It is a mixture of substances called hydrocarbons.

items.t: The living things that became crude oil lived in ancient seas.
items.d: They lived millions of years ago, even before dinosaurs existed.

items.t: Heat and pressure changed buried remains into crude oil.
items.d: Crude oil is also called petroleum.

items.t: The word petroleum means rock oil, or oil from Earth.
items.d: Petroleum is another name for crude oil.

items.t: An oil refinery separates crude oil into useful products.
items.d: Some of those products are fuels.

items.t: Wind begins because the Sun heats Earth's surface unevenly.
items.d: Uneven heating makes air move from place to place.

items.t: Windmills can use wind energy to pump water.
items.d: Water-pumping windmills were once used all over the United States.

items.t: A daytime sea breeze forms when cool air moves from water toward warmer land.
items.d: Warm air over the land rises, and cooler air rushes in to replace it.

items.t: At night, a coastal breeze can reverse because land cools faster than water.
items.d: The different cooling speeds change how the nearby air moves.

items.t: Wind turbine blades collect the kinetic energy of moving air.
items.d: Kinetic energy is the energy of motion.

items.t: Wind creates lift as it flows over turbine blades, making them turn.
items.d: The effect is similar to lift on an airplane wing.

items.t: Static electricity is an imbalance of electric charge on or inside a material.
items.d: Rub a balloon on your hair and the charge makes it stick to the wall.

items.t: When two materials touch, electrons can move from one material to the other.
items.d: That moving charge is what makes things feel zappy afterwards.

items.t: Rubbing materials together is the main cause of the static electricity we notice every day.
items.d: Sliding down a plastic slide can leave your hair standing up.

items.t: Static charge can make your hair stand up.
items.d: Each hair gets the same kind of charge, and like charges push each other apart.

items.t: A balloon rubbed on hair picks up extra electrons, so it becomes negatively charged.
items.d: That charge lets the balloon stick to a wall for a while.

items.t: Foam packing peanuts can cling to a cat's fur because of static electricity.
items.d: Charged things attract light, uncharged things nearby.

items.t: A static spark happens when built-up charge suddenly escapes. This is an electrostatic discharge.
items.d: You may feel a tiny snap after walking on a carpet and touching a door handle.

items.t: A lightning bolt is like an ordinary static spark, only much bigger.
items.d: Both are charge jumping across a gap to even things out.

items.t: Dry air lets static charge build up more easily than damp air.
items.d: That is why you get more zaps in dry winter weather.

items.t: Static charge stays on an object until it can flow away as a current or discharge.
items.d: Touching a metal doorknob gives it a path, so you feel the little zap.

items.t: The word electron comes from elektron, the Greek word for amber.
items.d: People noticed that rubbing amber could give it an electric charge.

items.t: In 1600, William Gilbert found that glass, wax and sulphur also make static when rubbed, not just amber.
items.d: So static is not special to amber. Many materials do it.

items.t: Charles Du Fay found two kinds of electric charge.
items.d: He named them after glass and resin.

items.t: A triboelectric series lists materials by the charge they tend to gain when rubbed.
items.d: Johan Wilcke made one in 1757.

items.t: A photocopier uses static electricity to put toner powder in the right places on paper.
items.d: This process is called xerography.

items.t: Inside a copier, a drum is given an even coat of static charge first.
items.d: A thin wire gives the drum its charge before copying starts.

items.t: Early copier drums used selenium, which holds charge in the dark but loses it when light hits it.
items.d: So bright parts of a page can wipe the charge away.

items.t: A copier shines light from your page onto the drum, leaving a hidden pattern of charge.
items.d: This invisible pattern is called a latent image.

items.t: Copier toner is a fine powder that gets a static charge by rubbing against tiny carrier particles.
items.d: It is the same rubbing trick as a balloon on hair.

items.t: Charged toner sticks to the parts of the drum with the opposite charge, which makes the picture show up.
items.d: Static attraction is doing the drawing.

items.t: A copier moves toner from the drum onto paper using pressure and static attraction.
items.d: The powder jumps from the drum to the page.

items.t: Lightning heats the air around it to about 30,000 degrees Celsius.
items.d: That is several times hotter than the surface of the Sun.

items.t: Thunder is the sound of air that was heated so fast by lightning that it made a shock wave.
items.d: The air shoves outward very quickly, and we hear a boom.

items.t: The main current surge in a lightning bolt can move at up to one third the speed of light.
items.d: Light moves about 300,000 km each second.

items.t: Lightning strikes somewhere on Earth about 44 times every second.
items.d: That adds up to nearly 1.4 billion flashes every year.

items.t: The most common kind of lightning stays inside the clouds.
items.d: Many flashes never reach the ground at all.

items.t: Airplanes are hit by lightning fairly often, but strikes are generally not dangerous to them.
items.d: So a flash near a plane is rarely a problem.

items.t: A lightning rod is a metal rod on a building that helps protect it from lightning.
items.d: It gives lightning an easy path to follow.

items.t: Most lightning rods are made of copper or a mix of metals that contains copper.
items.d: Copper carries electricity very well.

items.t: Benjamin Franklin came up with the lightning rod in 1749.
items.d: He wanted to protect buildings from lightning.

items.t: A lightning rod must be connected to the ground to work.
items.d: The wire leads the electricity into the earth.

items.t: On a flat roof, lightning rods are usually placed around the edge.
